title: Portrait of the Khalsa

lines: A STEEL BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED SWORD.
A NAME, A CODE, A FORM.
cards: A steel bowl of water and sugar. A double-edged sword stirring it while banis are recited.
Five Sikhs, themselves already initiated, conduct the rite, and those coming forward drink the amrit and have it sprinkled on their eyes and hair. From that moment they belong to the Khalsa.
Yesterday's portrait was the inner one, a face turned toward the Guru. Today the portrait gets a name, a code and a visible form.

teach.h: PURE: ONE LIGHT IN THE HEART.
teach.b: First, pure. Sikhs say khalsa means pure.

In a savaiya attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, in paraphrase: the one who remembers the ever-living light day and night, who brings no other but the One into the mind, in whose heart the full light shines, know that one as khaalas, pure.
Purity here isn't a spotless record. It's a heart with one light in it. Second, brave.
The Khalsa is remembered as saint-soldiers: ready to defend the weak, never to bully.
Courage in this portrait is aimed outward, at someone else's safety.
Third, disciplined. The Khalsa keep the five Ks, the daily prayers, and a code of conduct, the rehat, that rules out things like tobacco and adultery.
It's a discipline you can see on a crowded street: the turban, the kara, the bearing.
Fourth, generous. The hands that carry a kirpan also stir the pots in the langar and give a share of what they earn. And an honest note: not every Sikh has taken amrit.
Sikhs who haven't are still Sikhs, and for some the Khalsa is a commitment grown toward slowly, when they're ready. Pure, brave, disciplined, generous.

how: Sikhs who join the Khalsa take amrit in the amrit sanchar ceremony conducted by five initiated Sikhs, then keep the five Ks and the Sikh code of conduct (rehat); Sikhs who have not taken amrit are still Sikhs.

games.q: what does “portrait of the khalsa” mean?
o: a council of elders who lead the gurdwara
the soldiers who guarded the Gurus' court
the initiated Sikh community: pure, brave, generous

p: the initiation, stirred with a sword

s: every Sikh is automatically part of the Khalsa
the Khalsa are initiated with amrit; Sikhs who haven't taken it are still Sikhs.
a savaiya attributed to Guru Gobind Singh calls the one lit by the full light pure
in whose heart the full light shines: know that one as khaalas.
the Khalsa's discipline is meant to stay hidden
it's visible: the five Ks, the turban, the bearing.

games.q: on a crowded train, someone is being harassed. you hold the Khalsa's ideals. what do they point toward?
o: look away; it isn't your business.
step in calmly to protect the person.
start a fight to teach a lesson.
games.why: the saint-soldier ideal: courage aimed at someone else's safety, ready to defend the weak, never to bully.

practice: Let the traits pass, one per breath: pure, brave, disciplined, generous, and pick the one that asks the most of you today.
Pure might mean one honest motive; brave, one hard sentence said kindly; disciplined, one habit kept when it's inconvenient; generous, one thing given before anyone asks.
Breathe with your choice, and if you pray, offer that moment to God.

wordCard.voice: Portrait of the Khalsa. The initiated community of Sikhs: pure, brave, disciplined, generous, with one light in the heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the Khalsa, the initiated community; Sikhs say the word means pure.

carryVoice: Your line: khalsa means pure. One light in the heart, nothing hidden behind it. That's today, done.

sources.ref: 33 Savaiye, savaiya 1 (attributed to Guru Gobind Singh: pooran jot jagai ghat mai tab khaalas taahi nakhaalas jaanai)
